t:
Section 4365 of title 39, United States Code, is amended by adding a new subsection to read as follows:


“(d) 
In addition to other matter authorized by this section to be contained, enclosed, or inserted in second-class mail, there may be included, in accordance with uniform regulations which the Postmaster General shall prescribe, on the envelopes, wrappers, and other covers in which copies of publications are mailed, messages and notices of a civic or public-service nature, if no charge is made for the inclusion of such messages and notices on such envelopes, wrappers, and covers.”.

fable.w: The section directs the Postmaster General to prescribe uniform regulations governing civic or public-service messages on second-class mail covers, and under the definition a requirement or authorization to issue regulations counts as participation. The tempting reading is that this is a purely substantive postal provision with no outside party named, but the rulemaking mandate itself is the participation mechanism.
fable.s: in accordance with uniform regulations which the Postmaster General shall prescribe

qwen_block.w: This section authorizes the inclusion of civic messages on mail envelopes and grants the Postmaster General the authority to prescribe regulations regarding this practice. It does not require consultation with outside parties, public comment, or any form of participation by non-federal entities in the decision-making process. The regulatory authority is exercised solely by the federal official.
qwen_block.s: In addition to other matter authorized by this section to be contained, enclosed, or inserted in second-class mail, there may be included, in accordance with uniform regulations which the Postmaster General shall prescribe, on the envelopes, wrappers, and other covers in which copies of publications are mailed, messages and notices of a civic or public-service nature, if no charge is made for the inclusion of such messages and notices on such envelopes, wrappers, and covers.

opus.w: The section requires the Postmaster General to issue uniform regulations governing these messages. Under the definition, required rulemaking counts as participation, because rulemaking ordinarily brings in public notice and comment (as in Example 6). It is tempting to say "No" because no outside party is named as a consultant, and the civic messages themselves are not public input into a federal decision. But the rulemaking requirement is enough on its own.
opus.s: in accordance with uniform regulations which the Postmaster General shall prescribe
opus.b: The tempting reading is "No": the section only allows civic or public-service notices on mail covers, and no outsider is consulted. That reading misses one point. The definition counts "requiring rulemaking" as participation, and Example 6 labels "Yes" any statute that directs an agency to issue regulations. Here the Postmaster General "shall prescribe" uniform regulations.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends postal regulations to allow certain messages on mail covers without charge. It does not require the federal government to consult with the public, hold hearings, or form advisory committees before making a decision. The Postmaster General, a federal official, prescribes the regulations. The public is not involved in the decision-making process; they are merely permitted to use the mail service in a specific manner.
qwen_chat.s: In addition to other matter authorized by this section to be contained, enclosed, or inserted in second-class mail, there may be included, in accordance with uniform regulations which the Postmaster General shall prescribe, on the envelopes, wrappers, and other covers in which copies of publications are mailed, messages and notices of a civic or public-service nature, if no charge is made for the inclusion of such messages and notices on such envelopes, wrappers, and covers.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that allowing "messages and notices of a civic or public-service nature" on mail envelopes constitutes public participation because it allows the public to communicate. However, this is merely a change in postal regulations regarding what can be printed on mail covers for free; it does not involve the public in a federal decision-making process, nor does it require consultation, hearings, or advisory committees. The Postmaster General (a federal official) prescribes the regulations, and the public is simply permitted to use the mail service in a specific way. There is no mechanism for the public to influence a government decision.
